Golden prompts and regression test plan
transcript:
Header: Wed Mar 11 2026 15:00 PDT — 48 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Liam Ortega (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (Empirica Head of ML), Jonah Rivera (Empirica Eng Mgr), Ravi Desai (Empirica Security), Clara Su (Product)

Summary: Align on quality eval plan, golden prompts, workload sizing, and POC timelines.

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey team, thanks for carving out time. Quick round robin — who all's here?
[00:07] Maya Patel: Maya here. Jonah, Ravi, Clara — we are the core group.
[00:12] Alex Chen: Great, I'll give a 5 minute overview of how Redwood usually runs a 4 week POC and then Priya will lead the quality gating conversation.
[00:19] Priya Nair: Hi — main goals today: define success metrics, agree golden prompt coverage, what regression tests look like, and what data you need to send us to run baselines.
[00:28] Jonah Rivera: We wanna be realistic about latency expectations and also pinpoint hallucination tolerances. For our use case the downstream parser is strict — format errors break pipelines.
[00:36] Priya Nair: Understood. On format we typically run both syntactic checks and a schema-compare for structured outputs; that's in our quality harness.
[00:44] Liam Ortega: Quick note: our runtime can enforce model variants and automatic fallback if p95 spikes, so a combined cost/latency policy is doable.
[00:50] Maya Patel: Good — question: how do you define hallucination in the eval? We saw one previous vendor count anything not in the reference as hallucination which blew up numbers.
[00:58] Priya Nair: Yeah, we use a tiered definition: hallucination type A is fabricating facts that contradict reference ground truth; type B is extraneous plausible but unverifiable content. For POC acceptance we propose Type A < 2% on the golden set, Type B reviewed by SMEs with a grief threshold.
[01:14] Clara Su: Works for product, we can triage Type B cases. How many golden prompts should we shoot for?
[01:20] Priya Nair: Our recommendation: 50–80 golden prompts split across core intents — informational, transactional, and extraction. The golden set should include edge cases and adversarial phrasing. We can draft an initial 60 and iterate.
[01:34] Jonah Rivera: On regression tests — we need auto-run nightly against the golden set and a small load sweep. Can Redwood host those runs or do we need to schedule ourselves?
[01:42] Alex Chen: Redwood will run the initial nightly test as part of the POC on the hosted infra and then we can move to your Private VPC for pull-based runs if you prefer. We'll include the baseline CSV output and annotations.
[01:52] Ravi Desai: From security the VPC/on-prem options are critical; we need KMS integration and audit logs. SOC2 is fine but send the compliance pack.
[01:58] Alex Chen: We'll send SOC2 + ISO summary, and a redacted audit log sample. Noted on KMS — that's supported in Redwood Private.
[02:05] Maya Patel: Back to scoring — do you provide automated scoring or do we need manual review arrays?
[02:12] Priya Nair: It's hybrid. For format and extraction we do deterministic checks (schema match, token-level edit distance). For intent correctness and hallucination we provide annotation UI and a small sample of SME-reviewed labels (we recommend 200 labels for statistically meaningful precision/recall estimates).
[02:28] Jonah Rivera: For workload sizing — our production traffic averages 120 QPS peak for the intent system but typical is 20–30 QPS. For POC we can do a scaled-down sweep to 50 RPS to validate batching.
[02:42] Priya Nair: Ok that's helpful — we'll recommend a baseline run at 10 RPS, an intermediate at 50 RPS, and a stress sweep to your target of 120 QPS to observe degradation points. We will measure p50/p95/p99 latency and throughput (RPS) plus token cost per 1k tokens.
[02:57] Liam Ortega: Note that KV cache behaviour matters for session-style workloads — if your sequences have long contexts we'll instrument KV cache hit rates. Sorry, K-V cash mis-typo in my notes —
[03:04] Maya Patel: (laughs) heard that.
[03:07] Clara Su: On acceptance criteria — can we put concrete gates? For example: intent F1 >= 0.88 on golden set, format pass rate >= 99%, Type A hallucination <= 2%, latency p95 < 350ms on hosted baseline at 10 RPS.
[03:22] Priya Nair: Those are reasonable. We might caveat latency with sequence length and model variant — we'll include a matrix of sequence-length buckets (short <128 tokens, medium 128–512, long >512) in the benchmark template.
[03:35] Maya Patel: Sequence length usually sits in the medium bucket (most queries ~200 tokens). Tokenization differences across models can change costs — can you normalize token counts?
[03:42] Alex Chen: We'll report both raw token counts and normalized tokens per a common tokenizer we provide.
[03:47] Jonah Rivera: Regarding scoring approach — what's the pass/fail process? If model A meets all gates except hallucination by 0.5% over threshold, do we iterate or fail?
[03:55] Priya Nair: We propose a remediation loop: first run produces baseline and a regression report. If only one metric slightly misses, we agree on a remediation sprint (prompt tuning, prompt filtering, or small model variant) and run a second verification. Full fail only if multiple critical gates fail after remediation.
[04:12] Maya Patel: Sounds fair. Timeline?
[04:15] Alex Chen: Typical 4-week POC breakdown: week 0 (prep): data share, golden prompt draft; week 1: baseline runs and initial scoring; week 2: prompt tuning and regression harness; week 3: verification, handoff, and recommendations. We can compress to 3 weeks if Empirica provides fast data access.
[04:34] Clara Su: We need a clear deliverable at the end — a report with metric tables, golden set annotations, cost per 1M tokens estimate, and operational runbook.
[04:41] Priya Nair: We'll deliver that plus a recommended deployment configuration (hosted vs dedicated vs private) and an ops checklist for rollouts.
[04:50] Ravi Desai: For legal/procurement: if we do Private we need a short MOU for infra access. Also please put any data retention defaults in writing.
[04:59] Alex Chen: We'll include data retention and retention toggles in the POC contract.
[05:04] Maya Patel: A few technical clarifications — do you support function/tool calling and structured output enforcement? Our parser expects strict JSON-LD.
[05:11] Priya Nair: We support function calling and structured output; we'll use a schema comparator and checksum-based verification for JSON-LD fidelity. We'll flag any minor whitespace or order differences as non-fail if semantically equivalent.
[05:25] Jonah Rivera: Benchmarks: please include tokenized cost per query and end-to-end latency (from API gateway through Redwood runtime).
[05:33] Priya Nair: Yep, our benchmark CSV includes columns for requestid, sequence_length, model_variant, tokens_in, tokens_out, cost_estimate, p50, p95, p99 latencies, and error codes.
[05:44] Alex Chen: Anything else on golden prompts? We usually ask customers to annotate expected outputs for each golden prompt and then we create a 'tolerance matrix' that defines acceptable variations.
[05:54] Maya Patel: We'll aim to annotate 200 expected outputs for the 60 golden prompts to help with statistical significance.
[05:59] Priya Nair: Good. For regression tests we'll pair the golden set with a broader 1k sample that runs nightly; any drift beyond a set threshold triggers an alert and we snapshot the model variants used.
[06:12] Clara Su: On false positives for hallucination detection — what's your approach to minimize noise?
[06:17] Priya Nair: We use a combination of literal-match checks and semantic similarity with thresholding, plus human-in-the-loop verification for uncertain cases. We tune thresholds during baseline runs.
[06:27] Maya Patel: Ok that helps. On scheduling follow ups — can we get the benchmark template and security docs by tomorrow?
[06:33] Alex Chen: Yes, Alex will send SOC2 and security briefs today; Priya will upload the benchmark template and a starter golden prompt spreadsheet tomorrow morning.
[06:41] Jonah Rivera: We'll try to have the sample queries and logs to you by Friday. Also, for the Private test env we'll set aside 2 nodes for the peak stress test.
[06:50] Alex Chen: Great. Last item — competitor mentions? Any particular objections?
[06:53] Maya Patel: We looked at Anthropic and a Cohere pilot; concerns were around cost and how well they handled strict structured outputs.
[07:02] Priya Nair: Noted. We'll make sure the POC emphasizes format enforcement and cost-per-query comparisons.
[07:09] Alex Chen: I'll recap and list action items.
[07:12] Alex Chen: Recap: Redwood sends security pack and benchmark template; Empirica shares logs and sample queries; Redwood drafts initial golden prompt set; Priya runs baseline tests and reports latencies and hallucination metrics; set follow-up for week of Mar 16 for prompt review.
[07:30] Maya Patel: Thanks everyone, talk soon.
[07:33] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcription: some speaker labels may be slightly off and there are a few misheard words (e.g., "K-V cash" instead of KV cache) which don't change action items.
